29:He's the CEO of Nextory, a Nordic audiobook streaming company. Normally, getting that kind of data means messaging a colleague, waiting for them to run the query, format it, and send it back. Sometimes hours, sometimes longer. The kind of friction that, at the scale of a CEO's week, becomes invisible because it's just how things work.
33:Later, what struck him wasn't the speed. It was something else:
47:Nextory had reached the point a lot of growing companies reach without anyone naming it: the system worked, until it didn't. The data was there. The pipelines ran. Stakeholders got their numbers. Yet the friction kept compounding. Decisions stalled because someone's number didn't match someone else's. Teams used the same word for slightly different things and didn't know it. Knowledge lived in the head of whichever data engineer had been there longest.
53:It's a small sentence that inverts the usual instinct. The default move at this stage is to throw engineering at the symptoms: another pipeline, another dashboard, another data engineer. Ninos's claim - which Nextory had to learn before they could act on it - is that those moves don't address what's actually happening. What's happening is that the organization's understanding of its own data has gotten quietly inconsistent, and no amount of additional plumbing (or AI) fixes a definition that means three things to three different teams.
61:What Calle is describing isn't a tooling problem. The dashboards work. The SQL runs. The numbers come out. The problem is that what the numbers mean has drifted from what the company thinks it's measuring. That's what clarity problems look like when you're inside one. They don't announce themselves. They show up as a screenshot in your DMs.
75:I'd been seeing the Nextory job ad scroll past my LinkedIn feed for a while. I love books, I work in data, so the algorithm had decided I should see it. The role description was the kind every growing company writes at some point: we need someone who can do data things for us. But one detail in the ad stopped me. The role sat under the COO, not under IT.
81:Data is a business concern that happens to run on technology. When you put it under IT, you optimize for the part of the problem that's easiest to measure and starve the part that actually matters. The thing most organizations get wrong, Nextory had already gotten right.
87:And the skill that fixes architecture, modeling a business and its data so they mean the same thing, is rarer than the job market makes it look. For a long stretch, the industry taught data professionals to move data and store it, not to model it. An engineer can have ten years of experience, every year of it real, without one of those years touching this kind of work. That isn't a failing of the engineers; it's what the industry asked of them. But it means a job ad is unlikely to surface the person who can solve a structural problem, and a CV won't tell you whether it did.
91:Nextory had been thinking architecturally before I showed up. And the architectural thinking was the visible surface of something deeper. Where data sits in the org chart isn't an org-chart preference. It's a semantic decision: what "data" means to the organization. Every decision in this case study that follows is the same decision applied at a different layer: what entities the business has, what a customer means, what the platform should run on.
97:Once the engagement was underway, the work began the way I'd hoped: at the level of definitions, not pipelines. Gustaf did something most COOs delegate.
99:He took the entity definitions Nextory was working with, the formal, written-down names for the things the business actually runs on, customers and subscriptions and content and territories, and presented them to the leadership team, founders included.
105:The result was the case study's most diagnostic moment. When the leadership team compared notes, quietly, without anyone trying to win, they realized something:
109:This is one of those facts that sounds normal until you stop and think about it.
125:At Nextory, definitions and implementations are not two different things.
127:In most data platforms, they are. The definitions live somewhere, a wiki, a data catalog, a Confluence page, and the implementation lives somewhere else, in SQL files and dbt models and pipeline configs. They start aligned. They drift. Within a year or two, the documentation is wrong and nobody trusts it, because the only thing actually true is whatever the code is doing now.
133:This is what keeps definitions from becoming a paper product that drifts into irrelevance. There's nothing to drift away from, because there's nothing apart.
141:`In the old platform, we ingested data into structured tables (i.e. we had committed to a schema during ingestion), which always created issues when source schema changed. Also, each staging layer query was manually written, and as a consequence, most of these queries differed a bit regarding things like naming conventions, rules about what logical steps that were allowed in the staging layer, and overall query structure. This meant that every single time we had to modify or debug the staging queries, we had to spend a bit of extra time remember exactly how this particular source had been handled.
145:`One example is our data-contract-driven unpacking of the raw source data. We ingest the data raw from source with everything in a big JSON blob. Then we have a data contract for each source, owned by the data producing product team, that lists how this raw data should be unpacked into a structured format. The actual SQL that produces the structured tables with unpacked data is then auto-generated by scripts that read each contract and applies the contract rules to build the SQL.
147:This is the same shape as the leadership-definitions principle, applied one layer down. The contract is the definition. The SQL is its mechanical consequence. You don't maintain the SQL. You maintain the contract.
151:`In the new platform we instead focus just on the data contract, and can feel confident that every staging table will work exactly the same across all sources. We focus on the overall architectural principles rather than source-individual specifics.
155:`For me this is a huge shift in the ways of working as a data engineer. I think it's a big step up in maturity, and it's much better to be able to keep discussions within and outside the team focused on architecture rather than how specific data sources are handled.
163:Xiaoyan Zhang is Nextory's Head of Data. She joined after the methodology was already running, and she did not come in convinced. Three things bothered her at first. The first was the "why bother" question: if the system generates code that produces the same output a person would write by hand, what's different? The second was a concentration concern: if the generation step is load-bearing for the whole platform, you've concentrated the platform's maintenance into whoever owns that step. And the third, in her own words:
173:Calle and Xiaoyan together describe the same shift from opposite sides. Calle tells us what got replaced: hand-written staging queries with their fingerprints. Xiaoyan tells us what got preserved: the business logic, the transformations, the readable record of what the system is doing and why. Together they make the methodology defensible. You're not trading transparency for productivity. You're getting rid of the part of the work that was never the point.
181:The methodology I just described isn't the one we built on day one. It's what we landed on after a wrong turn that cost us about six weeks.
183:Here's what happened. We built the DAS layer (ingestion, raw-to-structured, representing the system perspective of the data) first, in full, before we had anything end-to-end. The reasoning seemed sound: get the foundation right, then build up. From inside the build, it looked like steady progress. Mappings deployed, schemas validated, contracts written. From the team's perspective, waiting for something concrete to look at, it looked like nothing.
185:The deeper problem was that depth-first ordering hid bugs that only an end-to-end pipeline can catch. The clearest example: a silent identifier collision I didn't find until I started building a thin DAR prototype (consumption/serving layer of the data) to look at the data end-to-end. Two records that should have been distinct were being merged into one because of how I'd composed the identifier. The bug had been in the DAS for weeks, invisible because nothing downstream was looking at it.
187:What I'd do differently is build the entire stack thin first. A skeleton at every layer that someone can look at, even if it's wrong. Then iterate against existing trusted reports where possible. Depth comes after the loop closes. The funny part: I'd written exactly this argument in From Business Question to Working Prototype in Hours years before the Nextory engagement. Knowing a thing in principle and doing it under pressure are different problems. Once that loop closed at Nextory, the acceleration was real. The trust that came with validation is what made everything afterwards possible.
191:`Data Ownership.`
195:`We now have clearer data ownership, which gives our teams a better understanding of their impact and faster recall when improvements are made to our service.
197:Behind that sentence is the data-contract example from §5, from the organization side. The contract isn't just a technical artifact. It's the unit of accountability.
203:`With a declarative data platform, our speed has increased significantly. We moved away from manual SQL and legacy ELT pipelines with little to no information about definitions, schemas, or data ownership. Changes that used to take days now take hours.
207:`For me this is a huge shift in the ways of working as a data engineer. I think it's a big step up in maturity.
223:That last sentence is the inversion-of-dependency-direction insight that I think will outlive the rest of this case study. Most platforms inherit the structure of the systems that produced the data, and business logic gets retrofitted on top. Nextory's platform inverts that: the business logic is fixed, and the production systems converge toward it. Calle, from the DE seat:
225:`Discussions within and outside the team focused on architecture rather than how specific data sources are handled.
227:That's the same shift Gustaf is describing, at the level of what gets talked about in technical meetings. The vocabulary moved from source-specific to architecture-general. The same words mean the same things across teams. The system stopped needing translators.
233:The "more importantly" is doing real work in that sentence. Most methodologies look great when you ship version one. The question is what they look like in year three, when half the team has rotated, the definitions have been pressure-tested by reality, and the original architects are no longer there to remember why something was built the way it was. Maintainability is the long-tail benefit. It's what makes a system compound instead of decay.
235:Read all of this together, and the throughline is fewer islands. Less informal knowledge in heads. Less drift between what one team means and what another team means. Less retrofitting of business logic onto whatever the production system happens to expose. The platform isn't doing anything fundamentally new at any one layer; it's keeping the layers in sync, on purpose, all the time.
251:Clarity over convenience. The default direction of growth, in any organization, is toward convenience. It's faster, in any given moment, to use the word everybody on the call already knows, even if the people on the call mean slightly different things by it. It's faster to write your own query than to look up whether someone has already written one. It's faster to keep the knowledge in your head than to write it down. Each instance is rational. The aggregate effect is the entropy Ninos is describing.
253:What Nextory chose was a long series of decisions where the convenient thing and the clarifying thing pointed in opposite directions, and the clarifying thing got chosen. The leadership-presentation moment, the entity definitions, the contracts at ingestion, the semantic layer, all of it. That's the work that doesn't show up on a roadmap and doesn't get a launch post. It's the work of choosing.
265:There's an industry conversation right now that goes roughly: "AI is changing everything in data." That sentence is true and also useless. Everything is too big. The interesting question is what AI changes about data work when the underlying foundation is good versus when it isn't.
305:Nextory hasn't finished. No growing company finishes. What they've done is build a foundation that lets the next decisions, about data ownership, about new sources, about how agents are integrated into the workflow, get made with more clarity and less drift than otherwise. The work continues. It's just continuing on different terrain.
315:`My plan moving forward is to build a knowledge layer that keeps track of our full platform, with a lineage graph of all assets and how they connect, enriched with human-curated structured context covering architecture, rules, gotchas and everything an agent will need in order to understand how to use the data.
317:He's describing what comes after the platform-as-a-foundation: the knowledge layer that sits above it, makes the platform self-describing for both humans and agents, and lets the next round of capabilities compound on what's already there. It's the natural next thing. It would have been impossible on the old platform.
319:What I keep coming back to, writing this, is that the most important shift at Nextory wasn't a technology shift, even though there's plenty of technology in it. It was a discipline shift. Nextory decided, several times, that the work of clarity was worth doing even though it was harder than the work of convenience. That decision is what made everything downstream possible.
323:Shadi, asking the company a question and trusting the answer. Xiaoyan, seeing that the business logic is still visible. Calle, knowing every staging table works the same way. Ninos, watching teams have shorter arguments about what numbers mean.
325:These are the same thing. They're what it feels like when an organization has decided to know what its own words mean.

7:You've probably had this experience. Someone on your team shares an AI demo where a chatbot writes a React component or explains a complex algorithm in seconds. You think, "Maybe I should try this for my data pipelines." So you open your AI assistant and ask it something real: "Write SQL to calculate monthly churn for customers who downgraded their subscription tier."
23:The gap has four dimensions. `Business domain knowledge`: what does "subscription" mean in your organization? Is it an event, an entity, or a relationship? AI sees `subscription_status` but doesn't know "active" excludes status values 3 and 4. `Architectural knowledge`: where does this table fit in the overall system? What's upstream, downstream? AI sees individual files, not the system they comprise. `Data contracts`: what should this data look like? Which fields can be NULL and under what circumstances? AI can't validate against expectations it doesn't know exist. `Process knowledge`: how do you test changes? What validation steps matter? Most data engineering processes live in tribal knowledge, not documented workflows.
27:But what about the 90% of data engineering before analytics? Staging transformations, business logic derivation, dimensional modeling, testing, validation? That work is still humans writing SQL in editors, AI relegated to autocomplete. Not because AI can't help - because those layers aren't structured for AI to understand.
29:If the gap is informational, the solution is architectural - not just at the consumption layer, but across the entire platform. Ad-hoc SQL scripts with implicit business logic and conventions living in engineers' heads give AI nothing to work with. Semantic models with clear definitions, data contracts specifying types and constraints, documented conventions, explicit layer separation - these give AI rules to follow at every layer, not just the last one.
31:Metadata-driven data architecture isn't new - dimensional modeling and Data Vault both formalize how to organize business concepts. What's new is making metadata executable and machine-readable: YAML definitions that generate transformation code, contracts that drive testing, conventions in formats AI agents can consume. A DevOps-inspired approach where metadata IS the implementation - documentation can't drift because it's the same artifact as the code. Your semantic model becomes a shared language between humans and AI. Your layer boundaries become semantic checkpoints. Your conventions become enforceable context. The principles behind designing for agentic experience apply directly.
47:In the staging layer - DAS - AI works as a `reader and investigator`. Translation fidelity: raw source data to clean, typed, well-documented staging tables. YAML data contracts define the rules. The agent works within them. The constraints are features: you can't accidentally inject business logic into pure staging.
61:A multi-group mapping bug exposed the problem. The agent spent four iterations patching symptoms before we forced a stop and traced the full architecture: YAML contracts fed a compiler producing JSON, which fed a calculation engine generating SQL for BigQuery. The bug wasn't in the mapping expression. It was in how the compiler handled multi-group joins - five interconnected issues that no expression-level patching would fix. The answer was a targeted architectural workaround, not a sequence of band-aids.
65:`The human-AI split.` Through practice, a clear division emerged. Humans provide what AI can't: domain knowledge, intent, judgment, and investigative direction. The engineer who knows historical data from the old platform uses different column names, or that certain NULLs are expected for unactivated subscriptions - that knowledge is irreplaceable.
69:This plays out as conversation. You tell the Kimball agent: "This is `factless_fact_order` with grain (order_key, fact_ts). base_plan_key can be NULL before activation. offer_key can be NULL when no campaign applies." The agent verifies grain across 4.4 million rows, profiles NULLs across every column, traces an anomaly where two base_plan values appear at the same timestamp to a source data issue rather than a SQL bug, and documents it. You provide business rules and judgment. AI provides systematic execution.
71:`Contracts as shared language.` YAML data contracts serve as the interface between human intent and AI execution. Each contract specifies a single source-to-staging transformation: which raw table to read, what fields to extract, how to type-cast them, what expected values look like. A Python generator reads these contracts and produces SQLX files that Dataform executes against BigQuery.
73:What makes this powerful for AI is the constraint, not the automation. The contract specifies what staging must produce. When the agent encounters a new source system - Kafka event streams, MySQL CDC data, MongoDB collections, BigQuery cross-project tables - the template tells it exactly what to verify and how. The structure eliminates a class of errors: no accidental business logic in pure staging. A 4-tier testing framework validates every contract's output: syntax validation through dry-run compilation, NULL detection across millions of records, and automatic root cause analysis for extraction errors.
75:Historical data alignment is where AI assistance provides the most leverage - and fails most instructively. Source systems don't follow the same conventions across eras: column names change, value encodings shift, fields captured now were never captured historically. The staging agent treats every historical alignment as a potential trap - always querying actual data distributions before assuming compatibility, never trusting naming consistency. Tedious, detail-intensive work that benefits enormously from systematic investigation.
77:`When it breaks.` The failure modes are consistent. `Patching without understanding` - proposing fixes without grasping root cause. `Context window limits` - complex investigations cause the agent to lose track of earlier findings. Declarative architecture pays off here: an agent that "forgets" mid-session can re-align by reading the semantic model, contracts, and column descriptions. Definitions in conversation history vanish when the context window overflows; definitions in the architecture persist for any agent to find. `Overconfidence in SQL` - queries passing syntax checks but embedding subtle logic errors (counter: validation against known test cases). `Moving too fast` - changing code without branching, assuming columns exist without querying, mapping from names rather than data.
79:Once caught, these mistakes get permanently internalized. Tell the staging agent that a source field has different semantics in historical versus current data, and that correction influences every subsequent mapping. Systematic retrospectives with agents - reviewing decisions, encoding corrections into workflows - turn individual fixes into durable process improvements. The learning compounds - exactly how institutional knowledge should transfer.
85:Engineers who document their columns today are building the infrastructure for AI collaboration tomorrow. Every semantic definition, data contract, naming convention, explicit grain definition - these aren't just good engineering practice. They're the context transforming AI from a plausible guesser into a genuine collaborator.
89:The semantic layer vendors are right that AI needs structured context - they've proven it for the last mile of analytics. The opportunity is extending that principle across the entire platform: staging, business logic, dimensional modeling, testing, validation. Not just AI that queries correctly, but AI that helps build and maintain the platform itself.
91:If you're building data platforms today, the highest-leverage investment isn't AI tooling. It's making your platform declarative. Semantic models with clear definitions. Data contracts specifying transformations and constraints. Documented conventions. Explicit layer separation.
93:If you want a Monday morning starting point, begin with testing. Write down how your team validates a new table or transformation today - grain checks, NULL analysis, foreign key integrity, edge cases. Hand that checklist and warehouse access to an AI agent. What you normally spot-check across three examples, the agent validates exhaustively across every row. You don't need a declarative platform to start - you need one process, documented clearly enough for an agent to follow. That single experience makes the rest of this article's argument tangible.
103:`The DAS agent:` "Respect the constraints. The contracts, the branch workflow, the test suite - they aren't obstacles, they're your safety net. The most productive thing you can do is work within the structure, not around it."
105:This methodology applies the principles from Designing for Agentic Experience to data engineering specifically. For related reading, see The Rise of the Model-Driven Data Engineer on why declarative architecture matters. For deeper dives into individual workflows, see companion posts on AI-assisted data mapping, contract-driven data transformation, and convention enforcement.

### Many-to-many relationships fixed

Pre-0.7.0, M:N relationship support had real correctness issues under INCREMENTAL ingestion strategy. 0.7.0 ships a hardened implementation:

- `M:N X-table reader rewritten` with fingerprint-based set-change detection.

- `INCREMENTAL truedelta aligned with FULL_LOG` for exact-tuple modeling. Within-batch transitions now emit historical rows correctly.

- `Set-oriented relationship views.` `view_<source>_has_<target>` now returns the active member set per source entity at the latest effective timestamp. The previous pair-oriented partitioning returned one row per source/target pair; the new partitioning ties all members of the latest set together so the view returns them as one set.

- `Forward-only emission under INCREMENTAL.` INCREMENTAL relationship pipelines no longer write `row_st = 'N'` rows for set transitions. Set membership changes are detected by the set-oriented view at query time rather than by row-level closer/opener emission. FULL_LOG continues to soft-delete rows for source-row disappearance.

- `Canonical test suite extended` to cover BigQuery in addition to PostgreSQL.

Customers running INCREMENTAL pipelines on M:N relationships may see different row counts than before. The new counts are the correct ones.

## Why the change log wins, and why it is the same decision as "DAB history is dated by extracted_at"

Start with the constraint that is already settled: DAB history is dated by `extracted_at`, which is `to_timestamp(cast(_dlt_load_id AS DOUBLE))`. That decision is only meaningful if a key can carry more than one `extracted_at` in the object DAB reads. If `das__staged` were latest-per-key, every row would carry exactly one `extracted_at` per key at any moment, daana's `entity_effective_timestamp_expression: extracted_at` would produce exactly one version per key per execute, and DAB's history would be a function of how often somebody ran the pipeline rather than a function of the data. Option A and the already-decided provenance rule are not two decisions; they are one decision looked at from two ends.

The property this buys is the one the blueprint calls reloadability and S2 calls non-volatility: "DAB and DAR must be rebuildable from DAS at any time without going back to the source." With a change log and `FULL_LOG`, dropping the whole DAB schema and re-executing reproduces byte-identical history, because every `eff_tmstp` is a value in a row and not a wall clock. Spike 2 finding 6 observed exactly this: with `entity_effective_timestamp_expression: das_load_ts`, "eff_tmstp in view_<entity>_hist IS the DAS load timestamp verbatim", and after appending a changed row with a later load timestamp, `view_CUSTOMER_hist` held both versions while `view_CUSTOMER` held only the new one. Spike 2 finding 8 observed the other half: `FULL_LOG` is idempotent against a source view holding two rows for the same key — runs 7 and 8 both left `CUSTOMER_desc` at 25 rows. The two spike findings together say that the log shape and daana's default strategy were built for each other.

The `__current` projection is not speculative and is not there because the blog has one. It is there because one of this system's own already-decided rules demands it: "each question is computed twice, from `das__staged` and from `dar__uss`, and the two must agree." Spike 1 measured what happens to that comparison over a log: two runs gave "240 rows / 120 distinct orders". `dar__uss` reflects DAB's current state, so the DAS-side computation of the same question must be over one row per key. Something has to deduplicate. The only question is where.

## The rejected options, at their strongest

**Option B — latest-per-key `das__staged`, history stays in `das__raw`** is the option with the best short-term ergonomics, and it should be argued seriously. Every question over DAS becomes a plain aggregate with no window function. daana's `FULL` strategy becomes safe, since spike 2 finding 10 confirmed `FULL` is correct against a one-row-per-key view. Nothing in the layer ever double-counts. And the claim that "history is not lost, it is in `das__raw`" is literally true: the parquet is append-only and every load is retained.

It fails on what "retained" has to mean. `das__raw` is one VARCHAR `payload` column. Recovering a historical version from it means re-applying the contract's casts by hand, outside the generator, which is the hand-written staging micro-decision the whole artefact exists to abolish — and it would be a *second*, divergent implementation of the same contract, so the drift the contract prevents comes back in the diagnostic path. Worse, the loss is silent and permanent in DAB rather than merely inconvenient. If two ingests land between two `daana-cli execute` runs, the intermediate version never becomes a `_desc` row, and no amount of re-executing recovers it, because the latest view no longer contains it. B3 ("every version retained, none overwritten") would then be satisfied only when the operator happened to run the DAB step at the right cadence. A time-variance guarantee that depends on scheduling is not a guarantee. B also cannot derive the log; A can derive both `__current` and, later, a per-load snapshot, from the log.

**Option C — log only, every consumer deduplicates** is the purest reading of S1. DAS captures and persists; a window function is arguably already an interpretation; one contract, one object, no naming argument. And it is cheap: a `QUALIFY` in a question is four lines.

It fails on the blog's central diagnosis, which is about the thirtieth file, not the first: "five different engineers have each made slightly different decisions… and the staging layer has quietly become a collection of undocumented micro-decisions." A dedup rule written by hand in each question is precisely such a micro-decision, and it is the *load-bearing* one, because it silently determines whether corrections win. It is also fatal to the parity check specifically: the DAS-side and DAR-side computations would embody two independently-written recency rules, so the check could agree for the wrong reason or disagree for a reason that is not a data defect. A parity check whose two sides do not share a definition of "current" is testing the person who wrote the SQL.

**Option D — the log in `das__staged`, the latest in a third schema** mirrors the blog's two target models as two datasets, which reads cleanly and makes the log-versus-current choice impossible to get wrong by mistyping a table name. It is the option I would take if the two projections had different owners or different refresh cadences. Here they do not. It costs a third schema in a two-schema layer that has already been decided (`das__raw`, `das__staged`), it breaks the convention that a contract's stem is "used in every schema of this layer" by putting the same stem in three schemas with three meanings, and it buys separation between two objects that are always generated together from one file and always in lockstep. Sibling objects in one schema express "same source, two projections" better than sibling schemas do.

**Option E — no contract in slice 1** deserves the most respect, because it is the blog's own advice against itself: "For three source tables, just hand-write the SQL and move on with your life… For thirty tables, the math flips." With one contract, the generator is more code than the SQL it emits, and every line of it is unpaid overhead against slice 1's actual question.

It fails on what slice 1 is for. A vertical slice exists to prove the *machinery* end to end, not to answer one question — the machinery is what gets widened, and conventions §5 forbids data vocabulary under `src/` precisely so that the machinery is proven generic rather than asserted to be. Hand-written staging for slice 1 means the second contract, not the thirtieth, is where the generator gets written, and it gets written against SQL that already encodes one table's accidents. It also means slice 1's data checks, its drift check and its parity check are all written against a hand-rolled shape and rewritten later. And it forfeits the property the ACID TEST is asking about at the exact moment it is cheapest to establish: "is your contract documentation that someone manually keeps in sync with custom SQL, or does it directly generate unpacking logic?" You cannot retrofit that; you can only start with it.

## Which projection gets the plain name

Given A, the plain name should be the log, and this is not a coin flip. Consider the two ways of pointing at the wrong object. Point DAB at `orders__current` when you meant the log: history silently degrades to one version per execute, nothing errors, and the loss is unrecoverable. Point a question at `orders` when you meant `__current`: the number is wrong by a factor of the load count, the parity check fails, and it is fixed by editing one line. The default must be the failure that is loud and recoverable. It is also what the layer's own principle says: S2 makes DAS the layer that retains everything, so the object carrying the layer's plain name should not be the one that drops rows.

## Two adaptations away from the blog that I want on the record

The blog composes a composite primary key into a `_pk` column with a `CONCAT` separator, and warns correctly that a missing separator merges `'A001'+'12'` with `'A0011'+'2'`. The work-before-the-answer case study reports the same class of bug found in production — "a silent identifier collision… the bug had been in the DAS for weeks, invisible because nothing downstream was looking at it." The right fix is not a better separator; it is not composing at all. `primary_keys` stays a *list*, and the list is consumed as a list — by `PARTITION BY` in `__current` and by the distinctness check — never concatenated. Identifier composition is a DAS→DAB boundary concern (integration-by-design puts the Owner+Type prefix in the reader cast), and daana's mapping YAML already takes `primary_keys` as a list (spike 2 finding 2). DAS therefore has no composed-key surface to get wrong.

The blog uses `SAFE_CAST` uniformly and lets `mode` drive only the test tier. In DuckDB there is a real choice between `cast` (raises) and `try_cast` (NULL), and I am choosing `try_cast` everywhere plus generated checks — deliberately, against the instinct that "strict" should mean "raises". A raising view is a view you cannot diagnose: the blog's own root-cause tree needs you to query the thing that is failing, and DuckDB's projection pushdown means a raising cast fires in some queries and not others, so the error is both fatal and non-deterministic in where it appears. `try_cast` keeps DAS readable at all times and moves strictness into three generated checks that are not optional: REQUIRED-null detection, cast-loss detection (raw text non-null but cast NULL — the blog's "EXTRACTION BUG" branch made mechanical), and payload-key drift (a key present in `payload` that no column declares — the "SOURCE CHANGED" branch). That is a strictly more informative gate than a raise, at the cost of only being loud when the gate runs, which I list as a consequence rather than hiding.

One further point about `mode` in this particular source: Northwind's `$metadata` marks thirteen of the fourteen Order properties nullable, so almost every column is `NULLABLE` and the null-detection tier guards only `OrderId`. It is tempting to declare `OrderDate` and `ShipCountry` REQUIRED because slice 1's question needs them. That would be a lie about the source, and S1/S5 forbid it: `mode` records what the *source* guarantees, not what we want. Our need for a non-null order month is a DAB and DAR requirement, and the check for it belongs there.

## Ordering, and why it must be the load time

`__current` orders by `extracted_at DESC`, never by a source timestamp such as `OrderDate`. The reason is the blog's stated requirement for the latest model: "If sources send incorrect data then corrections, 'latest' views automatically reflect the corrected state" — a correction arrives in a later load and must win even when the business date it carries is older. Load time is the only ordering under which that is true by construction, and it is the same value DAB dates its history by, so the two layers agree on what "later" means without either of them being told.

input.contextAndProblem:
DAS is the only layer in this system that faces something nobody here controls. Everything above it — the DAB model, the generated USS, the marimo page — changes because we decided to change it. DAS changes because a third party changed something without telling us, and the blueprint's answer to that is two postures in one layer, not one: S3, "Forgiving ingestion, strict unpacking. Accept whatever arrives; enforce structure at the boundary out," with both halves justified by the same sentence — committing to a schema at ingest turns every upstream change into lost data, and enforcing nothing on the way out turns every upstream change into a silent one. The forgiving half is already settled: dlt lands the whole source record as one JSON column into hive-partitioned parquet, and spike 1 proved that works (`columns={"payload": {"data_type": "json"}}` produced exactly one `json` column with zero child tables even over nested objects and arrays). What is not settled is the strict half — what the artefact that enforces structure is, what it may say, and what SQL it turns into.

The hard part is not the mechanics. It is that the blueprint and the blog appear to contradict each other here, and the contradiction is registered in the synthesis: blueprint S1 says DAS is "Capture and persist only. No business logic, no interpretation, no enrichment," while four posts put unpacking, type casting, renaming and view generation inside DAS. The synthesis names it plainly: "Either the blueprint's DAS is only the landing zone (and staging is unlabelled), or the staging step violates a stated absolute." Both this repository's blueprint and the design-of-analytical-systems post resolve it the same way — DAS "often manifests as two physical layers: a raw landing zone and a staging area" — so the resolution is that `das__raw` is the capture, `das__staged` is the boundary out, and the contract's whole job is to enforce structure without adding meaning. That is only tenable if the contract is *structurally incapable* of expressing meaning, which makes the closed type vocabulary and the absence of any expression key load-bearing rather than stylistic.

Three specific things about this system make the obvious answers wrong. First, DAS here is append-only by construction and nothing ever rewrites it, so after two loads `das__staged` holds two rows per source record — spike 1 measured 240 rows for 120 distinct orders after two identical runs, and its own open questions list this as undesigned: "Does DAB want the full append history, or a latest-version view? This changes whether das__staged is a plain cast view or a QUALIFY/ROW_NUMBER view." Second, the consumer of `das__staged` is not a person writing SQL but daana-cli, and spike 2 found that its two candidate strategies have opposite requirements: `FULL_LOG` is idempotent against a multi-row-per-key source view, while `FULL` "silently inserts one extra duplicate row into `<entity>_desc` per execute, forever, and NONE of the presentation views show it." So the shape of `das__staged` decides, invisibly, whether the layer above it corrupts itself. Third, this system computes each question twice, once from `das__staged` and once from `dar__uss`, and requires the two to agree — which means `das__staged` must be able to answer a question at one-row-per-key, or the parity check becomes a comparison between a change log and a current state that can never agree.

There is a fourth pressure that cuts against building any of this. The blog that defines the contract is explicit that contracts are overhead at small scale: "For three source tables, just hand-write the SQL and move on with your life... For thirty tables, the math flips." Slice 1 has exactly one table. Every argument for a generator here has to survive the fact that its own primary source says not to build one yet.

Finally, the blog's contract shape was designed for Kafka into BigQuery, and two of its concrete mechanics do not survive the move. `SAFE_CAST` does not exist in DuckDB, so the contract's `mode` has to mean something different than it did; and the blog composes composite keys into a `_pk` column with a `CONCAT` separator, which the same corpus reports as the source of a real production bug — "a silent identifier collision... The bug had been in the DAS for weeks, invisible because nothing downstream was looking at it." What travels and what does not is therefore part of the decision, not a detail of it.

Whether the CI protocol is a decision of this ADR or of the CI ADR. The safety of the two-object design depends entirely on CI replaying the fixture twice; with one replay the log and the current view are identical and none of this is tested. That protocol has to be owned somewhere explicitly.

data.argument:
## Why the change log wins, and why it is the same decision as "DAB history is dated by extracted_at"

Start with the constraint that is already settled: DAB history is dated by `extracted_at`, which is `to_timestamp(cast(_dlt_load_id AS DOUBLE))`. That decision is only meaningful if a key can carry more than one `extracted_at` in the object DAB reads. If `das__staged` were latest-per-key, every row would carry exactly one `extracted_at` per key at any moment, daana's `entity_effective_timestamp_expression: extracted_at` would produce exactly one version per key per execute, and DAB's history would be a function of how often somebody ran the pipeline rather than a function of the data. Option A and the already-decided provenance rule are not two decisions; they are one decision looked at from two ends.

The property this buys is the one the blueprint calls reloadability and S2 calls non-volatility: "DAB and DAR must be rebuildable from DAS at any time without going back to the source." With a change log and `FULL_LOG`, dropping the whole DAB schema and re-executing reproduces byte-identical history, because every `eff_tmstp` is a value in a row and not a wall clock. Spike 2 finding 6 observed exactly this: with `entity_effective_timestamp_expression: das_load_ts`, "eff_tmstp in view_<entity>_hist IS the DAS load timestamp verbatim", and after appending a changed row with a later load timestamp, `view_CUSTOMER_hist` held both versions while `view_CUSTOMER` held only the new one. Spike 2 finding 8 observed the other half: `FULL_LOG` is idempotent against a source view holding two rows for the same key — runs 7 and 8 both left `CUSTOMER_desc` at 25 rows. The two spike findings together say that the log shape and daana's default strategy were built for each other.

The `__current` projection is not speculative and is not there because the blog has one. It is there because one of this system's own already-decided rules demands it: "each question is computed twice, from `das__staged` and from `dar__uss`, and the two must agree." Spike 1 measured what happens to that comparison over a log: two runs gave "240 rows / 120 distinct orders". `dar__uss` reflects DAB's current state, so the DAS-side computation of the same question must be over one row per key. Something has to deduplicate. The only question is where.

## The rejected options, at their strongest

**Option B — latest-per-key `das__staged`, history stays in `das__raw`** is the option with the best short-term ergonomics, and it should be argued seriously. Every question over DAS becomes a plain aggregate with no window function. daana's `FULL` strategy becomes safe, since spike 2 finding 10 confirmed `FULL` is correct against a one-row-per-key view. Nothing in the layer ever double-counts. And the claim that "history is not lost, it is in `das__raw`" is literally true: the parquet is append-only and every load is retained.

It fails on what "retained" has to mean. `das__raw` is one VARCHAR `payload` column. Recovering a historical version from it means re-applying the contract's casts by hand, outside the generator, which is the hand-written staging micro-decision the whole artefact exists to abolish — and it would be a *second*, divergent implementation of the same contract, so the drift the contract prevents comes back in the diagnostic path. Worse, the loss is silent and permanent in DAB rather than merely inconvenient. If two ingests land between two `daana-cli execute` runs, the intermediate version never becomes a `_desc` row, and no amount of re-executing recovers it, because the latest view no longer contains it. B3 ("every version retained, none overwritten") would then be satisfied only when the operator happened to run the DAB step at the right cadence. A time-variance guarantee that depends on scheduling is not a guarantee. B also cannot derive the log; A can derive both `__current` and, later, a per-load snapshot, from the log.

**Option C — log only, every consumer deduplicates** is the purest reading of S1. DAS captures and persists; a window function is arguably already an interpretation; one contract, one object, no naming argument. And it is cheap: a `QUALIFY` in a question is four lines.

It fails on the blog's central diagnosis, which is about the thirtieth file, not the first: "five different engineers have each made slightly different decisions… and the staging layer has quietly become a collection of undocumented micro-decisions." A dedup rule written by hand in each question is precisely such a micro-decision, and it is the *load-bearing* one, because it silently determines whether corrections win. It is also fatal to the parity check specifically: the DAS-side and DAR-side computations would embody two independently-written recency rules, so the check could agree for the wrong reason or disagree for a reason that is not a data defect. A parity check whose two sides do not share a definition of "current" is testing the person who wrote the SQL.

**Option D — the log in `das__staged`, the latest in a third schema** mirrors the blog's two target models as two datasets, which reads cleanly and makes the log-versus-current choice impossible to get wrong by mistyping a table name. It is the option I would take if the two projections had different owners or different refresh cadences. Here they do not. It costs a third schema in a two-schema layer that has already been decided (`das__raw`, `das__staged`), it breaks the convention that a contract's stem is "used in every schema of this layer" by putting the same stem in three schemas with three meanings, and it buys separation between two objects that are always generated together from one file and always in lockstep. Sibling objects in one schema express "same source, two projections" better than sibling schemas do.

**Option E — no contract in slice 1** deserves the most respect, because it is the blog's own advice against itself: "For three source tables, just hand-write the SQL and move on with your life… For thirty tables, the math flips." With one contract, the generator is more code than the SQL it emits, and every line of it is unpaid overhead against slice 1's actual question.

It fails on what slice 1 is for. A vertical slice exists to prove the *machinery* end to end, not to answer one question — the machinery is what gets widened, and conventions §5 forbids data vocabulary under `src/` precisely so that the machinery is proven generic rather than asserted to be. Hand-written staging for slice 1 means the second contract, not the thirtieth, is where the generator gets written, and it gets written against SQL that already encodes one table's accidents. It also means slice 1's data checks, its drift check and its parity check are all written against a hand-rolled shape and rewritten later. And it forfeits the property the ACID TEST is asking about at the exact moment it is cheapest to establish: "is your contract documentation that someone manually keeps in sync with custom SQL, or does it directly generate unpacking logic?" You cannot retrofit that; you can only start with it.

## Which projection gets the plain name

Given A, the plain name should be the log, and this is not a coin flip. Consider the two ways of pointing at the wrong object. Point DAB at `orders__current` when you meant the log: history silently degrades to one version per execute, nothing errors, and the loss is unrecoverable. Point a question at `orders` when you meant `__current`: the number is wrong by a factor of the load count, the parity check fails, and it is fixed by editing one line. The default must be the failure that is loud and recoverable. It is also what the layer's own principle says: S2 makes DAS the layer that retains everything, so the object carrying the layer's plain name should not be the one that drops rows.

## Two adaptations away from the blog that I want on the record

The blog composes a composite primary key into a `_pk` column with a `CONCAT` separator, and warns correctly that a missing separator merges `'A001'+'12'` with `'A0011'+'2'`. The work-before-the-answer case study reports the same class of bug found in production — "a silent identifier collision… the bug had been in the DAS for weeks, invisible because nothing downstream was looking at it." The right fix is not a better separator; it is not composing at all. `primary_keys` stays a *list*, and the list is consumed as a list — by `PARTITION BY` in `__current` and by the distinctness check — never concatenated. Identifier composition is a DAS→DAB boundary concern (integration-by-design puts the Owner+Type prefix in the reader cast), and daana's mapping YAML already takes `primary_keys` as a list (spike 2 finding 2). DAS therefore has no composed-key surface to get wrong.

The blog uses `SAFE_CAST` uniformly and lets `mode` drive only the test tier. In DuckDB there is a real choice between `cast` (raises) and `try_cast` (NULL), and I am choosing `try_cast` everywhere plus generated checks — deliberately, against the instinct that "strict" should mean "raises". A raising view is a view you cannot diagnose: the blog's own root-cause tree needs you to query the thing that is failing, and DuckDB's projection pushdown means a raising cast fires in some queries and not others, so the error is both fatal and non-deterministic in where it appears. `try_cast` keeps DAS readable at all times and moves strictness into three generated checks that are not optional: REQUIRED-null detection, cast-loss detection (raw text non-null but cast NULL — the blog's "EXTRACTION BUG" branch made mechanical), and payload-key drift (a key present in `payload` that no column declares — the "SOURCE CHANGED" branch). That is a strictly more informative gate than a raise, at the cost of only being loud when the gate runs, which I list as a consequence rather than hiding.

One further point about `mode` in this particular source: Northwind's `$metadata` marks thirteen of the fourteen Order properties nullable, so almost every column is `NULLABLE` and the null-detection tier guards only `OrderId`. It is tempting to declare `OrderDate` and `ShipCountry` REQUIRED because slice 1's question needs them. That would be a lie about the source, and S1/S5 forbid it: `mode` records what the *source* guarantees, not what we want. Our need for a non-null order month is a DAB and DAR requirement, and the check for it belongs there.

## Ordering, and why it must be the load time

`__current` orders by `extracted_at DESC`, never by a source timestamp such as `OrderDate`. The reason is the blog's stated requirement for the latest model: "If sources send incorrect data then corrections, 'latest' views automatically reflect the corrected state" — a correction arrives in a later load and must win even when the business date it carries is older. Load time is the only ordering under which that is true by construction, and it is the same value DAB dates its history by, so the two layers agree on what "later" means without either of them being told.

Block style throughout: a column row has five keys and a prose `description`, so it exceeds §4's "about four keys" flow-style budget. `---` document start included (spike 4 finding 12: yamllint warns without it).

Validator rules over this file (all gate-blocking): every `primary_keys` entry matches a declared `target_name` (fixes the blog example's own dangling key); `target_name` equals the mechanical snake_case of the last segment of `source_path`, making conventions §1.1 machine-checkable rather than reviewer-checkable; `type` is in the closed vocabulary below; `mode` is `REQUIRED` or `NULLABLE` and nothing else; `raw_schema`/`staged_schema`/`models` equal the layer constants; no key named `expression`, `sql`, `filter`, `where`, `join`, `default` or `coalesce` exists anywhere in the document.

## 2. The type vocabulary and its DuckDB expressions

`P` is the `source_path`; the JSON path is `'$.' || P`. Spike 1 finding 15: `->>` yields VARCHAR, `->` yields JSON, both work directly on the VARCHAR `payload` column with an implicit cast.

| contract `type` | emitted expression | resulting DuckDB type |
|---|---|---|
| `STRING` | `raw.payload ->> '$.P'` | VARCHAR (no cast — `->>` is already VARCHAR) |
| `INTEGER` | `try_cast(raw.payload ->> '$.P' AS INTEGER)` | INTEGER |
| `BIGINT` | `try_cast(raw.payload ->> '$.P' AS BIGINT)` | BIGINT |
| `DECIMAL(p, s)` | `try_cast(raw.payload ->> '$.P' AS DECIMAL(p, s))` | DECIMAL(p,s) |
| `DOUBLE` | `try_cast(raw.payload ->> '$.P' AS DOUBLE)` | DOUBLE |
| `BOOLEAN` | `try_cast(raw.payload ->> '$.P' AS BOOLEAN)` | BOOLEAN |
| `DATE` | `try_cast(raw.payload ->> '$.P' AS DATE)` | DATE |
| `TIMESTAMP` | `try_cast(raw.payload ->> '$.P' AS TIMESTAMP)` | TIMESTAMP |
| `TIMESTAMPTZ` | `try_cast(raw.payload ->> '$.P' AS TIMESTAMP WITH TIME ZONE)` | TIMESTAMPTZ |
| `TIMESTAMP_SECONDS` | `to_timestamp(try_cast(raw.payload ->> '$.P' AS DOUBLE))` | TIMESTAMPTZ |
| `TIMESTAMP_MILLIS` | `to_timestamp(try_cast(raw.payload ->> '$.P' AS DOUBLE) / 1000)` | TIMESTAMPTZ |
| `JSON` | `raw.payload -> '$.P'` | JSON (nested object or array kept whole, uninterpreted) |

`TIMESTAMP_SECONDS` is the same template that produces `extracted_at` from `_dlt_load_id` — the provenance column is not a special case, it is one vocabulary entry applied to a non-payload source. There is no `REPEATED` mode and no flatten/explode type: an array that needs its own grain is its own OData entity set (`OrderDetails` is one), hence its own contract and its own landed table, because changing grain is a modelling decision, not a staging one. There is no `BOOLEAN_CDC`, no `COALESCE` and no `CASE` in any template — the dictionary is where future edge cases go ("the complexity lives in the dictionary, not in the loop"), and until one is needed the format is structurally incapable of expressing business logic.

## 3. `das__raw` — the forgiving layer

One view per contract over the append-only hive glob. Both `union_by_name => true` and `hive_types` are mandatory and both are in the emitted SQL.

```sql
-- Generated from das/contracts/orders.yaml. Do not edit; edit the contract.
CREATE SCHEMA IF NOT EXISTS das__raw;

CREATE OR REPLACE VIEW das__raw.orders AS
SELECT
    landed.payload AS payload,
    landed._dlt_load_id AS _dlt_load_id,
    landed._dlt_id AS _dlt_id,
    landed.extracted_on AS extracted_on,
    landed.filename AS source_file
FROM read_parquet(
    '/home/user/adss-2026-09-07/_lake/das__raw/orders/extracted_on=*/*.parquet',
    union_by_name => true,
    filename => true,
    hive_partitioning => true,
    hive_types => {'extracted_on': DATE}
) AS landed;
```

The column list is enumerated rather than starred (§3 forbids `SELECT *` in anything a consumer reads) and this loses nothing, because the loader — not the source — fixes this list: all source variability lives inside `payload`. `union_by_name => true` is still required, and for a stronger reason than the spike's: it is what lets the *loader's* own schema evolve without rewriting the lake, which S2 forbids. `das__raw` keeps dlt's names verbatim; DAS's own vocabulary begins at `das__staged`.

## 4. `das__staged` — the strict layer, the change log

```sql
CREATE SCHEMA IF NOT EXISTS das__staged;

CREATE OR REPLACE VIEW das__staged.orders AS
SELECT
    try_cast(raw.payload ->> '$.OrderId' AS INTEGER) AS order_id,
    raw.payload ->> '$.CustomerId' AS customer_id,
    try_cast(raw.payload ->> '$.EmployeeId' AS INTEGER) AS employee_id,
    try_cast(raw.payload ->> '$.OrderDate' AS DATE) AS order_date,
    try_cast(raw.payload ->> '$.RequiredDate' AS DATE) AS required_date,
    try_cast(raw.payload ->> '$.ShippedDate' AS DATE) AS shipped_date,
    try_cast(raw.payload ->> '$.ShipVia' AS INTEGER) AS ship_via,
    try_cast(raw.payload ->> '$.Freight' AS DECIMAL(18, 4)) AS freight,
    raw.payload ->> '$.ShipName' AS ship_name,
    raw.payload ->> '$.ShipAddress' AS ship_address,
    raw.payload ->> '$.ShipCity' AS ship_city,
    raw.payload ->> '$.ShipRegion' AS ship_region,
    raw.payload ->> '$.ShipPostalCode' AS ship_postal_code,
    raw.payload ->> '$.ShipCountry' AS ship_country,
    raw._dlt_load_id AS load_id,
    to_timestamp(cast(raw._dlt_load_id AS DOUBLE)) AS extracted_at,
    raw.extracted_on AS extracted_on,
    raw.source_file AS source_file
FROM das__raw.orders AS raw;
```

`payload` is deliberately absent. If it were here, a daana `transformation_expression` could read `payload ->> '$.X'` and bypass the contract entirely; leaving it in `das__raw` makes the strict boundary structural rather than advisory.

## 5. `das__staged.orders__current` — the deduplicated projection

```sql
CREATE OR REPLACE VIEW das__staged.orders__current AS
SELECT
    staged.order_id AS order_id,
    staged.customer_id AS customer_id,
    staged.employee_id AS employee_id,
    staged.order_date AS order_date,
    staged.required_date AS required_date,
    staged.shipped_date AS shipped_date,
    staged.ship_via AS ship_via,
    staged.freight AS freight,
    staged.ship_name AS ship_name,
    staged.ship_address AS ship_address,
    staged.ship_city AS ship_city,
    staged.ship_region AS ship_region,
    staged.ship_postal_code AS ship_postal_code,
    staged.ship_country AS ship_country,
    staged.load_id AS load_id,
    staged.extracted_at AS extracted_at,
    staged.extracted_on AS extracted_on,
    staged.source_file AS source_file
FROM das__staged.orders AS staged
QUALIFY row_number() OVER (
    PARTITION BY staged.order_id
    ORDER BY staged.extracted_at DESC
) = 1;
```

`x AS x` here is exactly the every-column-aliased discipline conventions §3 already excludes `AL09` for; spike 4 finding 6 confirms `AL09` fires on precisely this shape, and spike 4 findings 2 and 3 confirm the `duckdb` dialect parses `QUALIFY` where `postgres` cannot.

## 7. Emitted checks (all gate-blocking, all derived from the same contract)

```sql
-- key distinctness within a load: the primary_keys declaration is either true or it is a bug
SELECT staged.order_id, staged.load_id, count(*) AS rows
FROM das__staged.orders AS staged
GROUP BY staged.order_id, staged.load_id
HAVING count(*) > 1;                                   -- must be empty

-- REQUIRED nulls (one per REQUIRED column)
SELECT count(*) AS violations
FROM das__staged.orders__current AS cur
WHERE cur.order_id IS NULL;                            -- must be 0

-- cast loss: raw text present, typed value absent -> the contract's type is wrong
SELECT count(*) AS violations
FROM das__raw.orders AS raw
WHERE raw.payload ->> '$.Freight' IS NOT NULL
  AND try_cast(raw.payload ->> '$.Freight' AS DECIMAL(18, 4)) IS NULL;   -- must be 0

-- partition agreement: dlt's {YYYY}-{MM}-{DD} vs to_timestamp's UTC
SELECT count(*) AS violations
FROM das__staged.orders AS staged
WHERE staged.extracted_on <> cast(staged.extracted_at AS DATE);          -- must be 0

-- payload-key drift: reported, never failed. This is the forgiving half proving itself.
SELECT DISTINCT unnest(json_keys(raw.payload)) AS undeclared_key
FROM das__raw.orders AS raw
WHERE unnest(json_keys(raw.payload)) NOT IN (
    'OrderId', 'CustomerId', 'EmployeeId', 'OrderDate', 'RequiredDate', 'ShippedDate',
    'ShipVia', 'Freight', 'ShipName', 'ShipAddress', 'ShipCity', 'ShipRegion',
    'ShipPostalCode', 'ShipCountry'
```

`manifest.yaml` per entry: `url`, `http_status`, `odata_count`, `recorded_at`, `sha256`, `kind: recorded | derived`, and for derived entries `parent` and `mutation`. `adss das record` writes it; `adss das ingest --offline` resolves each request URL against it, verifies the body hash, and hard-errors on a URL with no fixture (never an empty page). Only the HTTP transport differs from a live run: the same resource, the same json-column hint, the same append disposition, a fresh `_dlt_load_id` per replay — which is what makes two replays of one recording produce two loads and therefore testable history, offline, in CI.
data.confirmation:
The decisive check is one CI test that replays the single recorded Northwind fixture **twice** into a fresh lake and a fresh DuckDB file, then runs the DAB step once, and asserts all of the following. Replaying twice is the whole point: with one load, the log and the current view are identical and every claim in this ADR is trivially satisfied, so a one-load CI proves nothing.

1. `SELECT count(*) FROM das__raw.orders` = 2N and `count(DISTINCT das__raw.orders._dlt_load_id)` = 2 — every load retained (S2).
2. `SELECT count(*) FROM das__staged.orders` = 2N, `count(*) FROM das__staged.orders__current` = N, and `count(DISTINCT order_id)` equal in both — the log is a log and the projection is a projection.
3. The generated checks in §7 of concreteShape all pass: zero key duplicates within a load, zero REQUIRED nulls, zero cast-loss rows, zero `extracted_on <> cast(extracted_at AS DATE)` rows.
4. `SELECT typeof(freight) FROM das__staged.orders LIMIT 1` = `DECIMAL(18,4)` — the strict layer recovered the precision dlt's inference would have lost (spike 1 finding 16).
5. Every declared `target_name` equals the mechanical snake_case of its `source_path`, and every `primary_keys` entry resolves to a declared column — asserted by the contract validator, not by a reviewer.
6. **The generation test (the ACID TEST made executable):** a neutral, non-Northwind fixture contract with K columns generates exactly K select expressions, and deleting one column from it makes exactly one select expression and one COMMENT statement disappear. This is what distinguishes a contract that generates from a contract that annotates, and it lives under `tests/` with a neutral model per conventions §5.
7. **The cross-layer proof:** replay a `recorded` fixture, then its `derived` sibling in which one order's `Freight` differs, then run `daana-cli execute` once. `dab.view_ORDER_hist` must hold two versions for that order with `eff_tmstp` equal to the two `extracted_at` values, and one version for every unchanged order. This is the single assertion that proves the log reached DAB as history rather than as a snapshot.
8. **Two structural gate rules:** no daana mapping `table:` value names an object in `das__raw`, and no mapping sets `ingestion_strategy: FULL`. Both are one-line greps over the mapping YAML and both close a silent-corruption class (spike 2 finding 9: `FULL` against a multi-row source adds one duplicate `_desc` row per execute, forever, invisible in every presentation view).

The decision has stopped holding the moment any of 1, 2, 6 or 7 fails, or the moment a hand-written `.sql` file appears under `das/` that is not generator output.

consequences.text: One artefact carries documentation, schema and transformation, so they cannot drift: adding a column to Northwind Orders is a five-line contract diff plus a regenerate, and the column's description, its cast, its null check and its warehouse COMMENT all move together. The blog's ACID TEST ('does it directly generate unpacking logic?') is passed by construction and is provable by a single machinery test.

Rebuild-from-DAS is deterministic. Because every eff_tmstp in DAB is a data value (extracted_at) rather than the wall clock of the run, dropping the whole DAB schema and re-executing reproduces byte-identical history. That is what makes daana's drop-and-redeploy upgrade path safe, and it is what blueprint S2 and the reloadability claim in design-of-analytical-systems actually require.

Corrections win automatically. Ordering __current by extracted_at DESC rather than by any source timestamp means a later load beats an earlier one even when it carries an older business date — the blog's stated requirement for a latest model — and it is the same ordering DAB uses, so the two layers cannot disagree about what 'later' means.

daana's FULL strategy becomes structurally unnecessary, so spike 2's silent-corruption bug is out of reach rather than merely avoided. FULL_LOG against the log is idempotent (spike 2 finding 8: 25 rows across runs 7 and 8) and produces exactly the history the build needs (findings 6 and 7).

The strict boundary is physical, not advisory: payload does not exist in das__staged, so no DAB mapping expression can reach past the contract into the raw JSON, and no consumer can accidentally depend on an undeclared source field.

das__staged.orders grows as loads x records with no compaction and no incremental predicate, and every consumer scans all of it. daana's FULL_LOG recomputes its true delta against the full log on every execute, so the DAB step is the first thing that slows down, and it slows down in proportion to how long the system has been running rather than to how much changed. Spike 1 explicitly did not measure this: 'Not tested at scale: 120 rows only... the cost of DuckDB scanning hundreds of small per-load parquet files was not measured.' Nothing in this design has a plan for compaction, and adding one later collides with S2's ban on rewriting.

Two objects per contract, and the more dangerous one has the shorter name. A question or a mapping that says das__staged.orders when it meant orders__current double-counts in exact proportion to the number of loads — and in a CI run that replays the fixture once, log and current are identical, so the mistake is invisible. The safety of this design rests on the CI protocol replaying twice, not on the schema. If someone 'speeds up CI' by dropping to one replay, the guard silently disappears.

__current means 'the latest version we ever received', not 'what the source has now'. A record deleted upstream stays in __current forever, and daana's FULL_LOG soft-delete never fires because the key never disappears from an append-only log. DAS as designed cannot express 'this key was absent from load N' at all; answering that needs a third projection nobody has designed. Anyone who reads 'FULL_LOG continues to soft-delete rows for source-row disappearance' and assumes deletes are handled will be wrong.

try_cast everywhere means a type violation is a NULL, not an error, until a check runs. Between two gate runs a REQUIRED column can be silently NULL all the way through DAB into a marimo page. The cast-loss check makes it mechanically diagnosable but only after the fact, and only if 'adss das check' is actually wired into every ingest rather than only into CI.

The generated SQL carries an absolute path to the lake (spike 1's gotcha: relative paths in a view resolve against the querying process's cwd, so a view created from the pipeline directory breaks when marimo opens the same file from elsewhere), so it cannot be a stable committed artefact. Reviewers see a contract diff and not a SQL diff, and reproducing the SQL requires running the generator. The DuckDB-variable alternative is closed off because daana-cli opens its own connection that we do not control.

For this particular source, mode does almost no work. Northwind's $metadata marks thirteen of fourteen Order properties nullable, so the null-detection tier guards only OrderId, and the strictness of 'strict unpacking' rests almost entirely on the type casts and the drift check. The contract will look more rigorous than it is until a source arrives with real REQUIRED fields.

Every contract repeats raw_schema, staged_schema and models, which are global facts. The validator forces them to equal the layer constants so a stale one fails the gate, but a schema rename is still a sweep across every contract file rather than a one-line change.

This ADR requires a clarification to conventions §1.1 before it can land cleanly: the rule 'columns this layer adds itself carry no source's word' has to be stated as applying at the das__staged boundary, because das__raw deliberately keeps dlt's _dlt_load_id and _dlt_id verbatim. Until that clarification is written, a reviewer reading §1.1 literally is right to block the das__raw view.

data.contextAndProblem:
DAS is the only layer in this system that faces something nobody here controls. Everything above it — the DAB model, the generated USS, the marimo page — changes because we decided to change it. DAS changes because a third party changed something without telling us, and the blueprint's answer to that is two postures in one layer, not one: S3, "Forgiving ingestion, strict unpacking. Accept whatever arrives; enforce structure at the boundary out," with both halves justified by the same sentence — committing to a schema at ingest turns every upstream change into lost data, and enforcing nothing on the way out turns every upstream change into a silent one. The forgiving half is already settled: dlt lands the whole source record as one JSON column into hive-partitioned parquet, and spike 1 proved that works (`columns={"payload": {"data_type": "json"}}` produced exactly one `json` column with zero child tables even over nested objects and arrays). What is not settled is the strict half — what the artefact that enforces structure is, what it may say, and what SQL it turns into.

The hard part is not the mechanics. It is that the blueprint and the blog appear to contradict each other here, and the contradiction is registered in the synthesis: blueprint S1 says DAS is "Capture and persist only. No business logic, no interpretation, no enrichment," while four posts put unpacking, type casting, renaming and view generation inside DAS. The synthesis names it plainly: "Either the blueprint's DAS is only the landing zone (and staging is unlabelled), or the staging step violates a stated absolute." Both this repository's blueprint and the design-of-analytical-systems post resolve it the same way — DAS "often manifests as two physical layers: a raw landing zone and a staging area" — so the resolution is that `das__raw` is the capture, `das__staged` is the boundary out, and the contract's whole job is to enforce structure without adding meaning. That is only tenable if the contract is *structurally incapable* of expressing meaning, which makes the closed type vocabulary and the absence of any expression key load-bearing rather than stylistic.

Three specific things about this system make the obvious answers wrong. First, DAS here is append-only by construction and nothing ever rewrites it, so after two loads `das__staged` holds two rows per source record — spike 1 measured 240 rows for 120 distinct orders after two identical runs, and its own open questions list this as undesigned: "Does DAB want the full append history, or a latest-version view? This changes whether das__staged is a plain cast view or a QUALIFY/ROW_NUMBER view." Second, the consumer of `das__staged` is not a person writing SQL but daana-cli, and spike 2 found that its two candidate strategies have opposite requirements: `FULL_LOG` is idempotent against a multi-row-per-key source view, while `FULL` "silently inserts one extra duplicate row into `<entity>_desc` per execute, forever, and NONE of the presentation views show it." So the shape of `das__staged` decides, invisibly, whether the layer above it corrupts itself. Third, this system computes each question twice, once from `das__staged` and once from `dar__uss`, and requires the two to agree — which means `das__staged` must be able to answer a question at one-row-per-key, or the parity check becomes a comparison between a change log and a current state that can never agree.

There is a fourth pressure that cuts against building any of this. The blog that defines the contract is explicit that contracts are overhead at small scale: "For three source tables, just hand-write the SQL and move on with your life... For thirty tables, the math flips." Slice 1 has exactly one table. Every argument for a generator here has to survive the fact that its own primary source says not to build one yet.

Finally, the blog's contract shape was designed for Kafka into BigQuery, and two of its concrete mechanics do not survive the move. `SAFE_CAST` does not exist in DuckDB, so the contract's `mode` has to mean something different than it did; and the blog composes composite keys into a `_pk` column with a `CONCAT` separator, which the same corpus reports as the source of a real production bug — "a silent identifier collision... The bug had been in the DAS for weeks, invisible because nothing downstream was looking at it." What travels and what does not is therefore part of the decision, not a detail of it.

The ACID TEST: a contract that annotates hand-written SQL does not count; it must generate the unpacking logic
The blog's own scale advice — contracts are overhead below roughly thirty tables — has to be answered, not ignored
